title: Emotional-Intelligence Claims Laboratory
summary: Six fictional measures - a self-report questionnaire, two tasks with scored answers, colleague ratings of social effectiveness, and the ordinary personality and reasoning measures any claim has to beat. Students read the correlation matrix, test how much of the pattern is method rather than content, run incremental validity properly, and judge five pieces of marketing against the evidence they have in front of them.
learningObjectives: Distinguish convergent evidence from correlation produced by a shared method of collection.
Explain what incremental validity asks that a raw correlation with an outcome does not.
Describe how self-report and maximal-performance measures of the same label can behave differently.
Judge a construct claim against convergent, discriminant and incremental evidence rather than against its plausibility.
Explain construct proliferation and why an attractive label can conceal divergent operational definitions.
interactionTypes: claim evaluation scored against current settings
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every correlation and regression runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it and produces no score for them.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, radios, checkboxes, a select and buttons throughout; every slider announces what it controls in words rather than as a bare number. The correlation matrix is an ordinary table whose cells state their correlation as a number and whose row headers name the collection method, so the tint and the dotted underline marking same-method pairs are reading aids rather than the only cue. The scatterplot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving the pair, the model correlation with a plain-language band, the correlation observed in the simulated sample and the variance shared. Judged claims state agreement in words as well as by border colour. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Construct validity: convergent, discriminant and incremental evidence, and what an attractive label can hide
simulationNotes: Six fictional measures described by method type rather than by name. No published emotional-intelligence questionnaire, task, item or scoring key is reproduced, quoted, paraphrased or scored, and no specific test is criticised. Correlations are model-implied: each measure is a weighted sum of independent sources - dispositional, emotion ability, general cognitive, a questionnaire method effect and a testing method effect - so the correlation between two measures is the sum of the products of their shared coefficients. Standardised regression weights are solved from that matrix by Gaussian elimination and the variance accounted for is reported from them. The self-report scale's content is a fixed amount of common variance split between two sources by one angle, so the mix slider redirects the scale without improving it. The numbers are chosen to make a teaching pattern visible and are not estimates of any published finding.
